surfaces.part: ramp surface (stepped treads seen from above)

answer.evidence: The silhouette is 48 px wide on all 32 rows, so it is a full rectangular tile. The column scans show olive tread bands separated by thin darker 1-row step lines at about rows 6, 10, 14, 19, 23 and 27. The surface gets lighter toward the bottom, which suggests a ramp descending away from the viewer. There is no vertical south face of 3 or more rows, only a few dark pixel columns at the left and right edges, which look like cut-wall shading. The whole tile is the ramp's top surface seen from above, so it reads as a top-down slab with no front face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a ramp of regular horizontal bands. Each band is a flat tan fill with a light top edge and a darker lower line, so it reads as about 4 lightness steps against the references' 5-6. It has no tufts, grain, speckle or per-stone shading, so the grass reference's clumps and the paving reference's stone-by-stone shading are missing. The measured facts are mixed. Visible tones per tile are 7, matching the paving reference. Near-flat coverage is 0%, but only because the band lines break up every 5x5 block. Only 11 distinct colours exist in total. 49% of the dark edge pixels are near-neutral, so the outline is partly a grey or black sticker line and partly tinted, which I call mixed. The result looks more like a stylised stripe pattern than a peat-cut surface with Beodeul-level texture, and it is thinner and more graphic than either reference. When in doubt, fail.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tan, stepped ramp made of horizontal bands. It has about 4 lightness steps and 11 colours in total, against roughly 6 steps and 80 colours in the grass reference. The measured facts look fine: 7 visible tones per tile (the paving reference also has 7), 0% near-flat coverage, and 49% neutral dark edge pixels, which reads as a mixed outline. By eye, though, each band is a smooth strip with a light top edge and a dark bottom edge, and there are very few grain dots, speckle or clumps inside the bands. It reads as a clean striped sticker, a bit like planks or thatch, with a dark border. It does not read as ground with soil or peat grain, and it has none of the per-element shading the references have. Nothing about it says peat cliff. A careful artist would find it thinner and flatter than the references, so it fails on the doubt rule.
